cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter \(\mathcal C\) on a finite ground set \(E\) is a family of subsets of \(E\), no one properly containing another. Its original members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover is a set \(T\subseteq E\) meeting every member, and \(	au(\mathcal C)\) is its minimum cardinality. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members; \(
u(\mathcal C)\) is its maximum cardinality. Deleting an element removes it from the ground set and discards all members containing it. Contracting an element removes it from the ground set and from every member, then keeps only inclusion-minimal members. A minor is obtained by any finite sequence of these operations, including the empty sequence. The packing property is \(	au(\mathcal D)=
u(\mathcal D)\) for every minor \(\mathcal D\). For the empty family both numbers are zero. For the degenerate minor \(\{\varnothing\}\), set both numbers to \(+\infty\): no cover exists and arbitrarily many copies of the empty member can be packed. These conventions give no obstruction from degenerate minors. For an original clutter and capacities \(w\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\), define \[	au_w(\mathcal C)=\min\left\{\sum_{e\in T}w_e:T\subseteq E	ext{ is a cover}ight\},\qquad 
u_w(\mathcal C)=\max\left\{\sum_{F\in\mathcal C}y_F:y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{\mathcal C},\ \sum_{F
i e}y_F\le w_e	ext{ for every }e\in Eight\}.\] Multiplicities \(y_F\) allow repeated packed members, and every copy consumes one unit of capacity at each of its elements. Both optima are finite because original members are nonempty. The max-flow min-cut (MFMC) property is equality of these optima for every nonnegative integer capacity vector; the weights and ground-set size have no fixed upper bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal implication, or of its logical negation. An affirmative answer must establish \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)=\nu_w(\mathcal C)\) for every clutter with the packing property and every nonnegative integer vector \(w\). A negative answer must exhibit a finite clutter and such a vector with \(\tau_w(\mathcal C)>\nu_w(\mathcal C)\), and verify the packing property for every minor. A finite census, a proper subclass theorem, or fractional duality alone is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

For the member-by-element incidence matrix \(A\), whose entry \(A_{F,e}\) is one precisely when \(e\in F\), the corresponding fractional problems are \(\min\{w^{\mathsf T}z:Az\ge\mathbf1,\ z\ge0\}\) and \(\max\{\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}y:A^{\mathsf T}y\le w,\ y\ge0\}\). The conjectured equality concerns integer solutions, and hence is stronger than ordinary linear-programming duality. It asks for integral optima on both sides for every integer weight.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

Roy and Saha report a proof for \((n-2)\)-uniform clutters: every member has size exactly \(n-2\) when the ground set has \(n\) elements. Arbitrary clutters can have unrelated member sizes, so this subclass result leaves the stated universal implication unchanged.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: General-alphabet Hamming oracles with optimal preprocessing
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic data structure which, for every pair of strings of lengths \(n,m\ge1\) and every integer \(1\le x\le\min(n,m)\), uses \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing time and stored words and answers exact substring Hamming-distance queries in \(O(x)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The strings \(A\) and \(B\) are supplied explicitly over \([0..(n+m)^2)\). A query \((i,j,\ell)\) satisfies \(0\le i\le n\), \(0\le j\le m\), and \(0\le\ell\le\min(n-i,m-j)\). It returns \(|\{t:0\le t<\ell,\ A[i+t]\ne B[j+t]\}|\). Positions are zero-based; a length-zero query returns zero. Set \(L=n+m\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The soft-O means multiplication by \((\log(L+2))^c\) for one fixed constant \(c\), independent of \(x,n,m\). One fixed algorithm receives \(x\) during preprocessing and handles all admissible parameters. The stored space includes both strings, if retained, and all auxiliary information. Query space is included; no offline knowledge of future queries is supplied. More explicitly, there must be constants \(C\ge1\), \(c\ge0\) and \(d\ge8\), independent of all input parameters, such that preprocessing uses at most \(C(nm/x)(\log_2(L+2))^c\) operations, total stored and query workspace uses at most that many words, and every query takes at most \(Cx\) operations. The constants can absorb the finitely many smallest inputs. No randomness or error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Hamming distance counts mismatched positions in two equal-length strings. Here the input is a fixed pair of longer strings, but each query chooses its own pair of starting positions and common length. The output is a single exact integer, so the query need not list the mismatches.

For example, with \(A=(1,2,1,3)\) and \(B=(1,3,1,2)\), the query \((0,0,4)\) returns two, while \((1,1,2)\) returns one. The starting positions may differ, and neither interval must be a prefix. Symbols are arbitrary integers in the specified range; their numerical differences have no role.

The parameter \(x\) specifies a family of preprocessing–query compromises for the same task. When \(n=m\), the target includes nearly quadratic preprocessing with constant query time at \(x=1\), and nearly linear preprocessing with linear query time at \(x=n\). Every intermediate value must be handled by the same uniform algorithm.

Boneh and coauthors obtain \(\widetilde O(nm/x)\) preprocessing and \(O(x)\) exact query time for constant alphabets. Their general polynomial-integer-alphabet bound is \(\widetilde O(nm/\sqrt{x})\) preprocessing with the same query time. The card retains the previously selected deterministic question of removing this preprocessing gap.

The paper also gives approximate randomized oracles. Their guarantees allow an error in the reported distance and therefore concern a different output requirement. The present proposition requires exact answers on every query and has no probabilistic success qualification.

The source lower bound assumes a hypothesis about combinatorial matrix multiplication and applies to combinatorial oracles. The target here allows all operations in the stated word RAM. That restricted conditional result therefore does not establish an unconditional optimum or refute the proposed general-alphabet bound.

cards.why: This isolates the cost of reusable exact similarity queries and tests whether large alphabets create an inherent preprocessing penalty.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the same model, quantifiers and resource guarantees. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion. An improvement that does not meet the full target is insufficient.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
